column2: The foreigners gather to fight Israel, and Achish tells David with emphatic certainty that both he and his men will accompany him. Know for certain carries the cognate emphasis.
David promises knowledge of what his servant will do, and Achish appoints him chief bodyguard all the days. The exchange's open-ended language remains without supplying David's unstated intention.
Samuel's death, national mourning and burial at his city Armathaim precede the reminder of Saul's removal of mediums and knowers. Both practitioner categories remain.
column3: Medium and knower are contextual provisional renderings, not a complete taxonomy of ancient practices.

column2: Foreigners camp at Soman and all Israel's men at Gilboa; the selected locations and complete muster remain.
Saul sees the camp, fears and experiences a greatly astounded heart; the bodily reaction remains rather than a new psychological diagnosis.
Inquiry through the Lord receives no answer in dreams, clear signs or prophets. The three channels remain distinct and clear signs is not silently replaced with a transliterated alternative text.
Saul seeks a female medium to approach and inquire through; the servants' There is presents the Endor woman. The inquiry's human intermediary is explicit.
Concealment, changed garments, two companions and nighttime arrival precede the request to divine and bring up the named person. The request is recorded as Saul's speech.
The woman presents Saul's destruction of the two practitioner groups and accuses the visitor of trapping her soul for death. Her wording destroyed remains distinct from removed in verse 3.
Saul swears by the Lord's life that no wrong will befall her in the matter; the ei clause is interpreted as a negative oath.
The woman asks whom to bring up, and Saul names Samuel; the chosen name is not supplied earlier than the request specifies.
The narrator says the woman saw Samuel, then she cries loudly and identifies Saul as the deceiver. The narrator's naming is retained without adding a theological explanation of the event.
The king asks whom she saw and she reports plural gods rising from the earth. The plural is not silently changed to one spirit or angel.
The report describes a man standing upright and wrapped in a double cloak; Saul recognizes Samuel and bows face to earth.
column3: Standing upright describes physical posture, not moral uprightness. Neither the woman's observation nor Saul's recognition is expanded with an interpretation of apparition identity.

column2: Samuel asks why he was disturbed to come up; Saul reports distress, warfare, God's departure and non-answer through prophets and dreams, then requests guidance.
column3: The selected narrator attribution Samuel remains, while reception theories belong outside the translation; no omitted clear-sign channel is added to Saul's shorter speech.

column2: Samuel challenges inquiry because the Lord departed and came to be with Saul's neighbor; neighbor is not changed to enemy or a different actor.
The Lord's accomplished action corresponds to speech by Samuel's hand, while tearing and giving the kingdom to David are future. The tense distinction remains.
Failure to hear and execute divine furious anger against Amalek explains this day's action. The explicit causal structure remains without an added doctrinal rationale.
Israel and Saul are delivered into foreign hands, Saul and his sons will fall tomorrow, and Israel's camp is delivered; the repeated handing-over remains.
column3: Will fall is not replaced by will be with me, absent from this selected text.

column2: Saul hastens and falls from standing, fears Samuel's words and lacks strength after eating no bread all day and night. Standing is physical and the fasting explanation remains explicit.
The woman sees his great haste, recalls hearing his voice and words and putting her soul in her hand. Behold and the repeated hearing remain.
column3: Hurried greatly follows espeusen; the contextual distress sense and unusual physical sequence remain open for lexical review rather than silently normalized.

column2: She asks reciprocal hearing, offers a morsel and commands eating for strength because he must travel. The source's conditional/practical purpose is retained without expanding the meal's effect.
Initial unwillingness gives way to servants' and woman's urging, then hearing, rising from the ground and sitting on the seat; both groups persuade.
A grazing heifer in the house is slaughtered, flour taken and kneaded, and unleavened cakes baked. Grazing is not replaced by fattened from another form.
Food is brought to Saul and servants, all eat and leave that night; the shared meal and final nighttime setting remain.
All foreign camps gather at Aphek while Israel camps at Aendor in Jezreel; the selected Aendor locality is not silently converted to a spring.
Satraps pass by in hundreds and thousands, with David's company at the rear with Achish. The marching arrangement remains rather than an invented total army size.
The satraps question the passing men, and Achish identifies David as Saul's servant and cites days, this being the second year, with no fault found since arrival.
column3: The second-year claim is retained beside chapter 27's four months; no calendar or narrative solution is asserted without evidence.

column2: Distressed generals demand return to the assigned place, forbid joining battle or plotting against the camp and fear reconciliation through the men's heads. The threat remains their reasoning.
Propose struck in place of struck down to match the same Greek song already translated at 18:7 and 21:12. The two numerical song lines receive authored line breaks within the question.
column3: This consistency revision does not deny battlefield death; it avoids adding a different verbal force to an otherwise identical recurring quotation.

column2: Propose For before Achish's explanation that he found no evil. His oath, favorable view of David and his movements, full time span and the satraps' opposing view remain.
The command to return in peace leads to emphatically not doing evil in the satraps' eyes; the evaluation is their viewpoint, not a generic narrator moral judgment.
David questions wrongdoing to Achish and anything found over the whole period that would bar him from fighting the king's enemies. The emphatic negative remains.
Achish reaffirms David's goodness in his eyes but quotes the satraps' prohibition; no comparison with an angel is inserted into this shorter selected reply.
Early rising includes David and his master's servants, return to the appointed place, rejection of a pestilent thought, renewed approval, early travel, light and departure.
column3: Thought interprets word placed in the heart; the singular instruction to David and plural travel commands remain recoverable from the explicitly named group.

column2: David and his men rise early to depart and guard foreign land, while foreigners ascend to fight Israel. Guarding is retained rather than merely returning to the foreign country.
